description: eXplorable Astronomical Record Viewer for Infrared Surveys
summary:
XARVIS (eXplorable Astronomical Record Viewer for Infrared Surveys) lets anyone explore real data from NASA’s SPHEREx telescope, which maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months. A 3-D viewer shows where SPHEREx is and what it can see. Double-click a point in the sky and XARVIS fetches every SPHEREx image of it from NASA/IPAC IRSA, measures it, and plays the images as an aligned time-lapse. Each source is checked against ESA Gaia DR3, CatWISE, Hipparcos and NASA/JPL catalogs; anything unexplained is flagged as a NEW object and can be tracked across the survey.

Impact: learning to access SPHEREx data took us over two hours of dense documentation; XARVIS makes it one click. Students can watch stars move, amateurs can shortlist unknown objects and researchers can check data quality, bridging amateur and professional astronomy in the search for Planet X.

Tools: Python (Flask, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, astroquery) and JavaScript/HTML/CSS, using only official NASA and ESA data. It runs on any laptop.

Creativity: frames from rotated detectors are aligned north-up into a time-lapse, coloured from two wavelengths taken at the same instant, and every analysis is projected back onto the 3-D sky.

We considered accuracy (positions match Gaia to ~0.5″; 45/45 motion checks pass), reliability during archive outages (retries, caching), speed (background jobs, instant reopen) and honesty (clear notes on display enhancements and detection limits).
details:
XARVIS (eXplorable Astronomical Record Viewer for Infrared Surveys) is a web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into something anyone can explore. A 3-D viewer shows SPHEREx's real orbit and what it can see on any date. Double-click the sky and XARVIS fetches every SPHEREx image of that patch from NASA/IPAC IRSA, measures each one, and plays them as an aligned time-lapse with time, wavelength, signal-to-noise and quality flags. Every source is compared with ESA Gaia DR3, CatWISE, Hipparcos and NASA/JPL catalogs; anything unexplained is flagged as NEW and can be tracked through every image that caught it.

Benefits and impact: accessing SPHEREx data took us over two hours of dense documentation; XARVIS makes it one click. Students see stars move, amateurs shortlist unknown objects for follow-up, and researchers check data quality before downloading, bridging amateur and professional astronomy in the search for Planet X.

Tools: Python (Flask, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, astroquery, pyvo) and JavaScript/HTML/CSS, on official NASA and ESA data only. Runs on any laptop.

Creativity: rotated detector frames are aligned north-up, coloured from two wavelengths taken at the same instant, and every analysis is projected onto the 3-D sky.

Factors: accuracy (positions match Gaia to 0.5 arcsec, 45/45 motion checks pass), archive outages (retries, caching), speed (background jobs, instant reopen), and honesty (notes on enhancements and detection limits).
